children: Japan and the U.S. agree on the global importance of an "orderly yen" and are continuing coordinated efforts in the currency market, Japan's finance minister said.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama's comments come as finance chiefs and central bank governors gather for a Group of 20 meeting that gives Tokyo and Washington an opportunity to signal policy alignment on foreign-exchange stability.
That messaging is being closely watched as the yen remains uncomfortably weak against the dollar, despite historic intervention by Japan and the U.S.

After meeting with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the sidelines of the G-20 gathering, Katayama said: "We confirmed that an orderly yen is essential for the stability of global financial markets, including the U.S., and that ongoing joint efforts between Japan and the U.S. will serve this shared objective."

The yen's persistent softness has added to market bets that the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates at its next meeting in September, a move that would help narrow the rate gap with the U.S. in the currency's favor.
The yen was last trading around 159.80 against the dollar, not too far from a 40-year low of nearly 164 that prompted joint currency intervention.

Speculation on rate hikes heightened following a report by national broadcaster NHK citing a senior U.S. official as saying that Bessent had spoken with Katayama and Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda about the need to show a path toward higher rates.
Speaking to reporters at the G-20 meeting, Katayama said that no such discussion had taken place and reiterated that it is up to the BOJ to decide on monetary policy.
